IDEA: Arbitration and non-tender triage. Owner: GM and baseball-ops analysts. Decision: tender, non-tender or trade each arbitration-eligible player before the late-November or early-December non-tender deadline, every offseason. Value at stake: each arbitration salary, plus the roster spot and replacement cost. Mechanism: compare the projected arbitration salary (driven by the arbitration process's emphasis on traditional stats) with projected next-season surplus value, and flag players whose run value is mispriced relative to their counting stats. Baseline: a public projection system plus a public arbitration salary estimate, with a gut call on borderline cases. Software: a ledger that ranks every arbitration-eligible player on the roster by projected surplus over a replacement acquirable at similar cost. Retrospective test: public arbitration salaries and public next-season performance.

ASSUMPTION: Arbitration outcomes reward counting stats more than run value, so a systematic gap between salary and value exists and persists.

ASSUMPTION: Non-tender decisions involve enough marginal cases each year for better ranking to change outcomes.

IDEA: Club-option and qualifying-offer decisions. Owner: GM and president of baseball operations. Decision: exercise or decline club and mutual options shortly after the World Series, and extend or withhold qualifying offers by the early-November deadline. Value at stake: option salaries, qualifying-offer salary exposure, and draft-pick compensation. Mechanism: estimate the probability that a qualifying offer is accepted and the player's free-agent market value from public contract history and the player's profile (age, injury record, agent). Baseline: accept the option if projected value exceeds its cost, and assume most qualifying offers are declined. Software: an acceptance-probability model and an option valuation calculator that includes the value of the compensation pick. Retrospective test: public qualifying-offer acceptance history and public contract data.

ASSUMPTION: Qualifying-offer acceptance is predictable from public features beyond what the simple "most decline" rule already captures.

ASSUMPTION: The number of option and qualifying-offer cases per year is enough to make this recurring rather than occasional.

IDEA: Free-agent contract pricing and winner's-curse correction. Owner: GM, president of baseball operations and ownership. Decision: bid levels and contract structures (years, opt-outs, deferrals) during the November-to-February signing window. Value at stake: the largest discretionary payroll commitments of each offseason. Mechanism: the club that wins an auction tends to overpay, so the club adjusts its bids for that, models aging curves with uncertainty bands, and prices opt-outs as options that benefit the player. Baseline: a public projection system, a dollars-per-WAR rule and crowdsourced contract estimates. Software: a contract valuation tool that discounts deferrals, prices opt-outs and estimates rival demand. Retrospective test: public contracts against realized public WAR.

ASSUMPTION: The dollars-per-WAR baseline mis-states the value of opt-outs and deferrals by enough to matter.

Baseline: extend after a strong breakout season, or extend top-ranked prospects. Software: an extension-timing model that compares the player's leverage curve with a skill-stability estimate. Retrospective test: public extension terms against counterfactual arbitration paths.

Mechanism: calibrate public prospect rankings and stat lines against later outcomes to find which ranking tiers and profiles the market systematically overvalues or undervalues. Baseline: trade partners and media price prospects by public top-100 lists and organizational rank. Software: a model that converts ranking history into an outcome probability, applied to trade candidates. Retrospective test: archived public rankings against realized MLB careers.

Value at stake: the full annual draft pool and the early-round surplus it buys. Mechanism: model signability and the expected value per bonus dollar by player type (college or high school, hitter or pitcher) using public draft history. Baseline: take the best player available on the club's board at slot. Software: a pool-allocation optimizer constrained by public slot values and signing rules. Retrospective test: public draft, bonus and outcome records.
